extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and deciding affidavits and declarations filed under 37 CFR 1.131 and 1.132 (evidence traversing rejections), including how to treat objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations), timeliness, nexus, probative value, and required examiner commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgment and commentary on admitted affidavits/declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: All admitted affidavits and declarations are acknowledged and commented upon by the examiner in his or her next succeeding action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The extent of commentary depends on the action taken; when the evidence overcomes the rejection, comments should be consistent with guidelines for statements of reasons for allowance (MPEP § 1302.14). If evidence is insufficient, the examiner must specifically explain why; general unsupported statements are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review for prior public use/on-sale and best mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Any affidavits or declarations submitted under 37 CFR 1.131 and the accompanying evidence must be reviewed carefully to determine whether they show that the claimed invention was 'in public use' or 'on sale' in this country more than one year prior to the effective filing date (statutory bar under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)); where the 1.131 evidence relies on an embodiment not disclosed in the application, the best mode question must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an affidavit overcomes a reference-based rejection, public use/on-sale activities may not be overcome under 37 CFR 1.131. A best mode rejection should be made only if the record, taken as a whole, establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that the specification has not set forth the best mode (see MPEP § 2133.03 and § 2165–2165.04).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132: form and examiner responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When any claim is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132; it is the responsibility of the primary examiner to personally review and decide whether such affidavits or declarations are responsive to the rejection and present sufficient facts to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All affidavits/declarations not falling under specific other rules are to be treated under 1.132. Use form paragraphs (e.g., 7.65, 7.66, and 7.66.01–7.66.05) as appropriate to state whether the affidavit is sufficient or insufficient and to explain reasons for insufficiency (untimely, fails to set forth facts, not commensurate in scope, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of evidence traversing rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence traversing rejections must be timely or seasonably filed to be entered and entitled to consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits/declarations and other evidence are considered timely if submitted: (1) prior to a final rejection; (2) before appeal in an application not having a final rejection; (3) after final rejection but before or on the same date of filing an appeal upon a showing of good and sufficient reasons why not earlier presented (37 CFR 1.116(e)); or (4) after prosecution is closed if filed with a request for continued examination (RCE) under 37 CFR 1.114 (or CPA for design applications). Untimely submissions may be refused entry (see In re Rothermel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of evidence and required explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence traversing rejections, when timely presented, must be considered by the examiner whenever present; all entered affidavits, declarations, and other traversing evidence are acknowledged and commented upon in the next succeeding action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner holds evidence is sufficient to overcome the prima facie case, comments should follow guidance for reasons for allowance. If evidence is insufficient, the examiner must specifically explain why—mere general statements (e.g., 'lacks technical validity' or 'not commensurate with the scope of the claims') without supporting explanation are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of objective evidence (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations containing evidence of criticality or unexpected results, commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc., must be considered by the examiner in determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations 'must always when present be considered en route to a determination of obviousness' (Stratoflex). Examiners must also consider comparative data in the specification intended to illustrate the claimed invention. Lack of objective evidence does not weigh in favor of obviousness, but failure to provide rebuttal evidence against an established prima facie case is dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement for secondary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To be of probative value, any secondary evidence must be related to the claimed invention (nexus required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must determine whether there is a factually and legally sufficient connection (nexus) between the objective evidence of nonobviousness and the claimed invention so that the evidence is probative. The weight attached depends on relevance and the amount/nature of evidence (see Ashland Oil v. Delta Resins & Refractories and Demaco).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence must be supported by actual proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence (unexpected results, commercial success, solution of a long-felt need, inoperability of the prior art, invention before the date of the reference, derivation allegations, etc.) should be factually supported by an appropriate affidavit or declaration to be of probative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere assertions or untested claims are insufficient; experimental data or factual support are required (see In re De Blauwe). Examples show lack of tests/comparisons undermines claims of unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney arguments cannot take the place of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The arguments of counsel cannot take the place of evidence in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney statements asserting unexpected results, commercial success, derivation, etc., are not evidence and must be supported by appropriate affidavits/declarations (see In re Schulze and MPEP § 2145).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion evidence: scope and weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual evidence is preferable to opinion testimony, but expert testimony is entitled to consideration and some weight so long as the opinion is not on the ultimate legal conclusion at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing expert opinion, consider the nature of the matter, strength of opposing evidence, expert's interest in the outcome, and presence/absence of factual support. Opinions on ultimate legal conclusions are not entitled to weight, but underlying factual bases may be persuasive (see In re Chilowsky, In re Lindell, Ashland Oil cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusory affidavits/declarations have limited weight
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration which states only conclusions may have some probative value but may have little weight when considered in light of all the record evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations should provide factual support rather than mere conclusions. Affidavits by applicants are less persuasive than disinterested persons but cannot be disregarded solely because of interest (see In re Brandstadter, Ex parte Keyes, In re McKenna).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing objective evidence against the prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant timely submits traversing evidence, the examiner must reconsider patentability; the ultimate determination must be based on the entire record by a preponderance of the evidence with due consideration to persuasiveness of arguments and secondary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence must be evaluated along with the facts supporting the prima facie case, not just against the conclusion itself. All competent rebuttal evidence taken as a whole should be weighed against evidence supporting the prima facie case. If still unconvinced, the examiner must state the reason(s) in the next Office action (e.g., commercial success not convincing or not related). See In re Oetiker, In re Piasecki, and related MPEP sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results: threshold and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Any differences between the claimed invention and the prior art may be expected to produce some differences; the issue is whether the properties differ to such an extent that the difference is really unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases assess whether differences are differences in kind vs degree; examiner must determine whether differences rise to the level of unexpectedness required to be probative (see In re Merck & Co., In re Waymouth, In re Wagner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater-than-expected (synergistic) results as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A greater-than-expected result is an evidentiary factor pertinent to the legal conclusion of obviousness/nonobviousness; synergism (effect greater than sum of components) can be persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must show results were greater than expected from the prior art to an unobvious extent and that the results are of significant, practical advantage. A greater-than-additive effect is not automatically sufficient if it could have been expected from prior art teachings (see In re Corkill, Merck v. Biocraft, Ex parte The NutraSweet Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority of a shared property as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that a claimed invention is unexpectedly superior in a property shared with the prior art can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No set number of examples is required; single-property unexpected superiority (with adequate support) may suffice (see In re Chupp and Ex parte A). Examiner should evaluate the significance and factual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of an unexpected property as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of a property not possessed by the prior art is evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing a new property can support nonobviousness but does not necessarily require a conclusion of nonobviousness without proper supporting evidence and weighting (see In re Papesch, Ex parte Thumm, In re Payne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of an expected property as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of a property which the claimed invention would have been expected to possess based on the prior art is evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrating that claimed compounds or inventions lack an expected property (supported by factual evidence) can be persuasive (see Ex parte Mead Johnson & Co.). Examiner must assess support and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on applicant to establish unexpectedness and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence relied upon should establish that the differences in results are unexpected and unobvious and of both statistical and practical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must explain and support proffered data; mere conclusory statements in specification or declarations are insufficient. See Ex parte Gelles, Ex parte C, In re Nolan, and In re Eli Lilly for examples of insufficient showings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative tests (direct and indirect) are probative
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct or indirect comparative tests of the claimed invention against the closest prior art, commensurate in scope with the claims, are probative of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative testing can rebut a prima facie case (see In re Boesch, In re Blondel, In re Fouche). For intermediates, applicant must identify the cause of unexpectedly superior activity in an end product and establish a nexus showing the intermediate is a 'contributing cause' (In re Magerlein).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing expected vs unexpected properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected and expected properties must be weighed in the final obviousness determination; expected beneficial results are evidence of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected properties must have significance equal to or greater than expected properties to overcome a prima facie case. Expected beneficial results may support obviousness (see In re May, In re Nolan, In re Eli Lilly, In re Gershon). Examiner must compare significance and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of nonobviousness must be commensurate in scope with the claims which the evidence is offered to support; results should occur over the entire claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data limited to a narrow subrange or a single species may be insufficient to support a genus or broad claim unless circumstances justify extrapolation. Examples: In re Clemens (temperature ranges), In re Peterson (aluminum alloy range), In re Grasselli (catalyst alkali metal comparisons). Under some circumstances a genus may be supported by species data, but examiner must evaluate commensurability.
